title: Learning to Cook Cantonese Food with My Grandma

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Grandma, I'm ready to learn the beancurd stick stew. Walk me through it?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: First, soak the dried beancurd sticks in warm water. Thirty minutes. Not hot, warm.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Thirty minutes? That's a long time. Is there a faster way? Like using hot water?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Hot water makes them mushy. You want them soft but still holding shape. Why do you always question my methods?

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I'm not questioning you. I just want to understand the science behind it. There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: 'Science'? This is cooking, not a lab. I've been making this for forty years. That should be enough.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I know you've been cooking forever. I just learn better when I know why something works.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Fine. Hot water breaks down the protein too fast. Warm water rehydrates gently. Happy now?

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That actually helps. Should I cut the ribs while we wait?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Yes. Small pieces, along the bone. And slice two thick pieces of ginger. Not thin strips.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Why thick? Thin would distribute the flavor more evenly, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Thin burns in the hot pan. Thick holds up. Must you argue about every single step?

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I'm not arguing. I'm asking. There's a difference. You taught me to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: I taught you to listen. There's a difference too. The pan is hot. Sear the ribs now.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Okay, ribs are in. They smell good. How long do I sear each side?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Two minutes each side. Don't move them around. Let them brown.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Should I add the ginger now or after the water?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Now. With a splash of cooking wine. Then water to cover. About two cups.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Two cups exactly? Or just enough to cover?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Enough to cover. I said about two cups. You don't need to measure everything like a robot.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I just want to get it right. I'm nervous I'll mess it up and waste the ingredients.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: ...You're not going to mess it up. Just relax. Add the beancurd sticks now. Cut into one-inch pieces.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Got it. One-inch pieces. Should I stir them in gently?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Yes, gently. They break easily. Let it simmer for forty minutes. Lid on, slightly open.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Forty minutes. Should we start the soup too, or is that too much at once?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: We can do both. Boil water in the other pot. Pork bones, carrots, red dates, goji berries.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: How much goji? A handful?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: About a tablespoon. Too many and it's too sweet. And soak the dried mushrooms.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Wait, mushrooms? You didn't mention mushrooms. What kind?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Shiitake. I told you at the start. Were you even listening?

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I was listening. You said beancurd, ribs, ginger. You didn't say mushrooms.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: I did say mushrooms. You were too busy asking why about everything else. Just soak them.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Okay. Soaking the mushrooms. The soup water is boiling. Bones first?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Blanch them first. Two minutes, dump the water, then fresh water. This removes impurities.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Blanching seems like an extra step. Does it really make a difference?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Yes, it makes a difference. The soup is clearer and cleaner. Stop treating my methods like suggestions.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I'm not treating them like suggestions. I'm trying to understand so I can do it on my own someday.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: ...I know. I'm sorry. I get defensive when someone questions my kitchen. Old habit.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: I get it. And I'm sorry too. I ask too many questions. Let's just cook.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Add the carrots, dates, and goji to the fresh water. Simmer for an hour. The stew needs oyster sauce now.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Two tablespoons of oyster sauce? And a pinch of salt?

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Taste first. Then decide. That's the real lesson. Not memorizing steps.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: It tastes really good. Maybe just a tiny pinch more salt. The beancurd soaks it up.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: Good instinct. Let it rest for ten minutes. Then we eat.

utterances.speaker: granddaughter
utterances.text: Thanks for teaching me, Grandma. Even when I drive you crazy.

utterances.speaker: grandmother
utterances.text: You don't drive me crazy. You remind me of myself when I was young. Too many questions, too much fire.
